questions.stem: In business planning, how is a 'business opportunity' best defined?
options: A gap or need that a firm can meet at a profit
Any new idea that the owner happens to like a lot
A loan that a bank has offered to the firm
A product that a rival already sells well

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can spot business opportunities in Jamaica, giving examples from at least three different sources.
essays.modelAnswer: Opportunities usually come from change, from problems and from gaps. A manager should keep scanning the business environment, using tools such as PESTLE as a checklist. Changes in the economy create openings: for example, rising remittances and a growing number of visitors increase spending on services such as tours, transport and local food. Changes in law and government policy matter too: a ban on some single-use plastics opens a market for reusable or biodegradable packaging, and incentives for agro-processing can make new food products worthwhile. New technology creates opportunities such as online ordering, mobile payments and delivery services for small shops. New infrastructure, such as a highway, cuts travel times and opens day trips and new delivery routes. Customers' complaints and frustrations are another rich source: long queues, unreliable service or products that are hard to find all point to unmet needs. The manager can also learn from staff, suppliers, trade fairs and business networks, and by watching what is succeeding in other countries. The key is to note each possible opportunity and then screen it with evidence, rather than acting on the first idea.
markingPoints: Explains that opportunities come from change, problems and gaps; uses scanning tools such as PESTLE
Example from economic or social change
Example from legal, policy or infrastructure change
Example from technology or customer complaints
Names other sources (staff, suppliers, networks, overseas trends) and the need to screen with evidence

essays.stem: Use SWOT and PESTLE to evaluate the opportunity for a Kingston transport firm to start a shuttle service between New Kingston hotels and the airport, and give a justified decision.
essays.modelAnswer: Inside the firm, its strengths may include experienced drivers, existing vehicles and maintenance, and a known name. Weaknesses may be a small fleet, no tourism experience and limited cash. Outside, the opportunities include steady business travel and visitor numbers, hotels wanting a reliable partner, and online booking. Threats include taxi operators and ride-hailing apps, hotel shuttles already in place, and fuel price rises. A PESTLE scan adds detail: political and legal factors include licensing and insurance rules for carrying passengers to the airport, which must be checked first; economic factors include fuel costs and the exchange rate, since many visitors pay in US$; social factors include visitors' expectations of safety and punctuality; technological factors include booking apps and vehicle tracking; and environmental factors include traffic and the option of fuel-efficient vehicles. On balance, the opportunity is promising if the firm can secure the necessary licence and agreements with two or three hotels before buying more vehicles. I would recommend a pilot with existing vehicles for three months, with clear targets, before any larger investment.
markingPoints: Sensible strengths and weaknesses for the firm
Sensible opportunities and threats in the market
PESTLE factors applied, including licensing and insurance checks
Weighs the factors to reach a balanced view
Justified decision, such as a conditional go with a pilot and targets

essays.stem: A firm could launch a mobile coffee service. Fixed costs are J$450,000 a month, the price is J$600 a cup, the variable cost is J$300 a cup, and expected sales are 2,000 cups a month. Calculate the break-even point, the margin of safety and the expected monthly profit, and recommend whether to go ahead.
essays.modelAnswer: The contribution per cup is the price less the variable cost: J$600 minus J$300 equals J$300. The break-even point is fixed costs divided by contribution: J$450,000 divided by J$300 equals 1,500 cups a month. The margin of safety is expected sales less break-even: 2,000 minus 1,500 equals 500 cups, which is 25% of expected sales. Expected profit is total contribution less fixed costs: 2,000 times J$300 equals J$600,000, minus J$450,000, which gives a profit of J$150,000 a month. These figures show the service can be profitable, and sales could fall by a quarter before it makes a loss. However, the margin is not large, and the figures depend on the sales estimate. Before going ahead, I would test that estimate with a short trial at one or two busy locations, check permits and food safety requirements, and see whether costs such as fuel and staff could rise. If the trial confirms sales of around 2,000 cups, I recommend going ahead, while watching sales weekly against the break-even level.
markingPoints: Contribution J$300 and break-even 1,500 cups
Margin of safety 500 cups (25%)
Expected profit J$150,000 a month
Interprets the figures, noting reliance on the sales estimate
Justified recommendation with a test or conditions (trial, permits, monitoring)

essays.stem: Evaluate the advantages and risks of moving fast to seize an opportunity compared with waiting to gather more information.
essays.modelAnswer: Moving fast can bring the benefits of being first: winning loyal customers, securing the best locations or partners, building a name before rivals arrive, and sometimes charging higher prices while there is little competition. Some opportunities only exist for a short time, such as a large event, a contract offer or a gap left by a competitor closing, so waiting means losing them. The risks are that decisions are made on weak evidence, costs and demand may be misjudged, systems may not be ready, and the firm may have to educate the market at its own expense while others copy its idea. Waiting allows better research, a tested product, clearer finance and a chance to learn from others' mistakes. But information is never perfect, and a firm that waits too long may find the window closed. The best approach is usually to move quickly but in a controlled way: gather the key facts that matter most for the decision, test with a small pilot or minimum viable product, commit limited resources at first, set clear measures and an exit point, and scale up once results are proven.
markingPoints: Advantages of moving fast: first-mover benefits; short windows
Risks of moving fast: weak evidence, misjudged costs, unready systems, copying
Advantages of waiting: better research and learning from others
Risks of waiting: window closes; perfect information never comes
Balanced conclusion: act quickly but with controls (key facts, pilot, limited commitment, measures, exit point)

essays.stem: Describe how a small firm can find the money, people and partners it needs to seize a large opportunity at short notice.
essays.modelAnswer: For money, the firm should first update its cash flow forecast to see how much it needs and when, since a large order often means paying for materials and staff long before the customer pays. It can then approach its bank for short-term finance such as an overdraft increase or order or invoice finance, using the confirmed contract as support. It can ask the customer for a deposit or stage payments and ask suppliers for longer credit. Owners may add capital, and development finance agencies may help with suitable projects. For people, the firm can use overtime carefully, hire temporary or contract staff with clear terms, and bring in specialists on short contracts, while making sure that new staff are trained and supervised. For partners, it can subcontract part of the work to a trusted firm, form a joint venture for a larger bid, or work with a distributor or retailer who already reaches the market. Each partnership should be set out in a written agreement covering roles, quality, payment and confidentiality. Throughout, the firm must avoid taking on more than it can deliver well.
markingPoints: Money: update cash flow forecast to find the size and timing of the need
Money: suitable sources (bank short-term or order finance, deposits, supplier credit, owner capital)
People: overtime, temporary or contract staff and specialists, with training and supervision
Partners: subcontracting, joint ventures, distributors, with written agreements
Avoids overcommitting beyond what can be delivered well

essays.stem: Explain how a firm can test an opportunity at low cost before committing fully.
essays.modelAnswer: The firm should first decide what it most needs to learn: usually whether customers will buy at the planned price, and whether it can deliver at the planned cost. It can then choose quick, cheap tests. Short interviews or a survey with likely customers show interest, but stated interest is weak evidence, so tests that involve real buying are better. Taking pre-orders or deposits, or offering the product at a market stall, a trade fair or a pop-up stand, shows whether people will actually pay. A minimum viable product, a simple first version with only the essential features, lets the firm learn from real users before investing in the full design. A pilot in one area or with one client tests delivery, costs and quality on a small scale. Online adverts or a simple web page with a sign-up button can measure interest cheaply. Each test should have a clear target set in advance, such as 50 pre-orders in a month, so the result is judged fairly. The firm should record what it learns, adjust the offer, and only commit full resources when the evidence supports it.
markingPoints: Decides first what most needs testing (demand at price, delivery at cost)
Uses low-cost tests; notes that real buying is stronger evidence than stated interest
Examples: pre-orders, deposits, stalls or pop-ups, MVP, pilot, online sign-ups
Sets clear targets in advance for each test
Records learning, adjusts, and commits fully only when evidence supports it

essays.stem: An opportunity to sell a new product has been approved. Plan the main steps to launch it within 90 days.
essays.modelAnswer: In the first two weeks, I would appoint a launch leader, confirm the objectives and budget, and draw up an action plan with tasks, owners, milestones and dates, shown on a Gantt chart. Legal and practical checks come first: permits, product approvals, labelling, insurance and contracts with suppliers. In weeks three to six, the focus is on getting ready to deliver: securing supplies and stock, setting up production or service processes, recruiting or training staff, setting prices, and preparing systems for orders, payments and records. Marketing preparation runs in parallel: defining the target market, the key message and the channels, preparing materials, and lining up any partners or retailers. In weeks seven to ten, I would run a soft launch with a small group of customers to test the product and processes, gather feedback and fix problems. In weeks eleven to thirteen, the full launch takes place, with promotion, and the team monitors sales, costs, customer feedback and stock daily at first. Weekly progress meetings keep the plan on track, and a review at day 90 compares results with targets.
markingPoints: Appoints a leader; sets objectives, budget and an action plan with milestones (e.g. Gantt chart)
Completes legal and practical checks early
Prepares delivery: supplies, processes, staff, pricing, systems; marketing in parallel
Soft launch or test, with feedback and fixes
Full launch with close monitoring, weekly progress checks and a 90-day review

essays.stem: Explain how a manager should identify and manage the risks of a new venture, including deciding when to stop.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager should list the risks with the team, covering demand (customers do not buy), finance (costs higher, cash runs short), operations (supplies, staff, quality), competition (rivals react), and legal, safety and reputation risks. Each risk is rated for likelihood and impact, and the main ones are given a response: reduce it, for example by a pilot or a fixed-price supplier contract; transfer it, for example through insurance or a partner; or accept it with a plan. Each risk has an owner, and the risk register is reviewed regularly. Financial exposure can be limited by starting small, investing in stages, and keeping a cash reserve. Before starting, the manager should agree clear measures of success and an exit point, such as sales below break-even for three months running, or losses above a set amount. When an exit point is reached, the team must decide honestly whether to change the offer, pause, or stop, without letting money already spent drive the decision. Agreeing the exit point in advance makes it easier to stop a failing venture before losses grow.
markingPoints: Identifies a range of risks (demand, finance, operations, competition, legal and reputation)
Rates likelihood and impact; chooses responses (reduce, transfer, accept) with owners
Limits exposure: start small, staged investment, cash reserve
Sets measures of success and an exit point in advance
Decides honestly at the exit point, ignoring sunk costs

essays.stem: Describe the legal and ethical points a firm must check before seizing a new opportunity in Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: The firm must first check that it has the right legal form and registrations: a new company is registered under company law, and the venture may need its own tax registrations, such as for GCT where it applies. Many activities need licences or permits, for example food handling, transport of passengers, tourism services, building work or selling alcohol, so these must be confirmed with the relevant authorities. Products must meet safety, standards and labelling rules. If the venture will employ staff, it must follow employment law on contracts, pay, hours and safe working conditions, and make statutory deductions. If it collects customers' personal information, it must handle it in line with the data protection law. The firm should protect its own brand names, designs and ideas under intellectual property law, and make sure it is not copying anyone else's. Contracts with partners and suppliers should be written and checked. Ethically, the firm should be honest in its marketing, treat customers, staff and suppliers fairly, avoid harm to the environment and the community, and refuse any bribes or improper favours. Professional advice is wise where rules are unclear.
markingPoints: Legal form and registrations (company law, tax registrations)
Licences, permits, product safety and labelling rules
Employment law and data protection obligations
Intellectual property: protect own and respect others'; written contracts
Ethical points (honest marketing, fairness, environment, no bribery) and seeking advice

essays.stem: Justify how a manager should monitor a newly launched venture and decide whether to grow it, change it or close it.
essays.modelAnswer: A new venture is uncertain, so close monitoring lets the manager spot problems and opportunities early, before losses grow or chances are missed. She should set a small number of measures linked to the plan: sales volume and value against target and break-even, gross margin, cash position, customer numbers and repeat purchases, customer feedback, and any quality or delivery problems. These should be reviewed weekly in the first months and monthly once the venture settles. She should compare actual results with the targets and ask why any gap exists. Customer comments and staff observations add meaning to the figures. If results beat targets and demand is steady, she can justify growing it, for example by adding locations or products, while checking that cash and quality can keep up. If results are below target but customers show interest in a related offer, she should change the product, price or market and test again. If results stay below the agreed exit point despite changes, she should close the venture in an orderly way, meeting obligations to customers, staff and suppliers, and record the lessons learned.
markingPoints: Justifies close monitoring (uncertainty, early warning)
Sets measures linked to the plan (sales vs target and break-even, margin, cash, customers, quality)
Reviews regularly and investigates gaps, using feedback as well as figures
Clear criteria to grow, change, or close (linked to the exit point)
Orderly closure meeting obligations, and lessons recorded

practical1.title: Screen three business opportunities and choose one
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group short briefs on three possible opportunities for a made-up small firm (for example a mobile coffee service, a tour package for cruise visitors, and a delivery service for rural shops). As a group, screen all three and choose the best one. Give each member a named role: market analyst (target market, competitors and evidence of demand), finance analyst (break-even, margin of safety and payback from the figures given, each checked twice), risk and legal analyst (main risks, permits and legal checks in general terms), strategy lead (builds a weighted scoring matrix and leads the decision), and writer (one-page decision memo to the owner). In a group of four, the strategy lead also writes the memo. Produce a SWOT poster and a PESTLE poster for your chosen opportunity. Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Three opportunity briefs with figures from the assessor
Flipchart paper and markers for the posters
Computer with spreadsheet and word processor software, and a printer
photos: The weighted scoring matrix for all three opportunities
The finance analyst's workings (break-even, margin of safety, payback)
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the screening
Used evidence from the briefs rather than opinion
Calculations are correct and were checked twice
SWOT and PESTLE points are relevant and placed under the right headings
Scoring criteria and weights are sensible and applied consistently
Decision memo gives a clear, justified choice with the main risks and next steps
safety: Use only the made-up firms and figures given
Respect each member's view; disagree with ideas, not people
Keep marker pens capped and the work area tidy
Share the workload fairly and take short breaks

practical2.title: Plan a 90-day launch and pitch it to an investor panel
practical2.brief: Using the opportunity your group chose in Practical 1 (or one given by the assessor), plan its launch and pitch it to an investor panel. Produce: a 90-day action plan as a Gantt chart with milestones; a launch budget and simple cash flow for the first three months; a resource and partner plan (money, people, partners); a pilot test with a clear target; and a slide deck of no more than 8 slides. Give each member a named role: project planner (Gantt chart), finance lead (budget and cash flow, checked twice), resources and partners lead, marketing lead (target market, message, launch channels and pilot test), and lead presenter. In a group of four, the project planner also prepares the resource plan. Every member presents part of the 8-minute pitch and answers at least one question from the panel (the assessor and members of another group). Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet and presentation software
photos: The launch budget and three-month cash flow on screen
The pilot test design with its target
The group pitching to the panel
checklist: Took a named role and produced their part of the launch plan
Gantt chart shows realistic tasks, owners, milestones and dates within 90 days
Budget and cash flow are correct, show the timing of cash, and were checked twice
Resource plan names realistic sources of money, people and partners
Pilot test has a clear target set in advance
Spoke clearly in the pitch and answered a question with evidence
safety: Use made-up figures only; do not present real firms' confidential information
Treat the panel and other groups with respect during questions
Keep projector and extension leads out of walkways
Agree a fair share of work and take a short break before the pitch
